ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌正式开源gBench基准评估框架，该工具旨在支持Gemma及其他开源模型的深度评估。gBench内置86个评估套件，涵盖聊天模板检查、代理基准测试及多层级的压力测试，旨在为开发者提供标准化的模型性能验证环境。

elements_zh.what: 发布开源评估框架gBench，包含86个评估套件
elements_zh.why: 解决行业内大模型评测标准碎片化的问题

elements_en.what: Released gBench, an open-source evaluation framework featuring 86 test suites
elements_en.why: To address the fragmentation of AI evaluation standards across the industry

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 谷歌通过发布gBench试图确立开源模型评测的话语权，通过内置大量代理任务测试，引导市场关注焦点从单纯的参数规模转向模型在复杂代理行为上的鲁棒性。此举将有助于加速闭源与开源模型在垂直领域性能对比的透明化。
ai_analysis.insight_en: By releasing gBench, Google seeks to establish influence over open-source model evaluation standards. By incorporating extensive agentic task tests, they are steering market focus away from parameter counts toward the robustness of models in complex agentic behavior, thereby accelerating transparency in performance benchmarking between open and closed models.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: 谷歌正式开源gBench基准评估框架，该工具旨在支持Gemma及其他开源模型的深度评估。gBench内置86个评估套件，涵盖聊天模板检查、代理基准测试及多层级的压力测试，旨在为开发者提供标准化的模型性能验证环境。

key_points_zh: 开源86项评估套件，涵盖代理性能与响应检查
支持Gemma及广泛开源生态模型评估
建立标准化测试基准以提升模型开发透明度
key_points_en: 86 open-source evaluation suites covering agentic performance
Support for Gemma and a wide range of open-source models
Establishing standardized benchmarks to improve model development transparency
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 谷歌通过发布gBench试图确立开源模型评测的话语权，通过内置大量代理任务测试，引导市场关注焦点从单纯的参数规模转向模型在复杂代理行为上的鲁棒性。此举将有助于加速闭源与开源模型在垂直领域性能对比的透明化。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: By releasing gBench, Google seeks to establish influence over open-source model evaluation standards. By incorporating extensive agentic task tests, they are steering market focus away from parameter counts toward the robustness of models in complex agentic behavior, thereby accelerating transparency in performance benchmarking between open and closed models.

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Good evening, fam 💜

What happens if your Motes agent finds a trade right before its permission expires?

Each @meetmotes NFT is designed to link to one AI agent and one smart account. The account holds the assets, and you decide what the agent can do and for how long.

Say you give your agent permission to make a swap until 6 PM. It prepares one at 5:59 PM, but the account checks it at 6:01 PM.

That swap should be blocked. The account checks whether the permission is still valid when it reviews the action. Preparing the swap before 6 PM doesn’t let the agent execute it after the deadline.

Think of it like an access pass. When the pass expires, you still own the account. The agent just needs your approval again before it can make a new move.

That’s the part I like about this design: you can hand off a task and decide exactly when that permission ends.

top_three.content_snippet:

top_three.summary_en: Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan is accused of planting recording devices in executive conference rooms, capturing hundreds of audio files including sovereign government briefings and confidential customer data. Prosecutors allege he utilized OpenAI’s internal tool, Codex, to configure the devices for voice-activated recording and automated exfiltration, with judicial proceedings now underway.
paragraphs: A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device at the company captured dozens of internal meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Monday.

The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, sorted into folders by date and renamed according to their contents, prosecutors said. Many of the recordings involved what appeared to be confidential trade secrets, including meetings with OpenAI customers, they said, and OpenAI identified others as containing material protected by attorney-client privilege.

The filing, which opposes Mr. Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before trial, offers the most detailed account yet of what investigators say he recorded. It also comes days after prosecutors told a federal judge that they were “not aware of any” evidence that Mr. Alfozan had committed espionage, stolen trade secrets or acted as an agent of a foreign government.
Prosecutors did not say in Monday’s filing that he had shared the recordings with anyone. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation,” they wrote.

Mr. Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, has been charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations and has pleaded not guilty. A hearing on his release is scheduled for Tuesday morning.

His lawyer, David Rizk, argued in a filing last week that the case had turned out to be far less serious than prosecutors initially suggested, describing his client as “an overly curious tinkerer.” Mr. Rizk wrote that the vast majority of recordings on Mr. Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”
Mr. Rizk could not be immediately reached for comment on Monday.

According to prosecutors, the recordings span 15 folders dated Sept. 8 to Sept. 28 and include meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room. One file was titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify the foreign government.

Mr. Alfozan used Codex, an OpenAI A.I. tool, through his wife’s account to help configure the recording device, add voice detection so it would “only record speech,” and move recordings through a Dropbox account, prosecutors said. His wife has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Prosecutors also said he photographed each printed page of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company in the early hours of Oct. 5. That was the same day a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team had found the listening device days earlier.

The filing also described Mr. Alfozan’s contact with Saudi officials. On Oct. 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent him a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based A.I. company, and asked: “Time to move back to KSA and join us?”

Mr. Alfozan suggested he might do so “after the IPO,” prosecutors said. The night before his Oct. 9 arrest, he spoke with the Saudi official by WhatsApp for 16 minutes. Prosecutors said he had also exchanged WhatsApp messages with officials at Saudi Arabia’s communications ministry, including the minister in August and September.

The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot
top_three.summary_en: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot officially attributed the cyberattack on over 700 European supermarket refrigeration controllers to Iran's 'SHAHID KAVEH' cyber unit during a G7 meeting. The attack, occurring between October 11-12, caused widespread equipment failures, fires, and tens of millions of euros in food losses, marking a transition from espionage to physical infrastructure sabotage.
paragraphs: French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Tehran of orchestrating the attack, warning that Iran would face retribution. Speaking Monday at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Paris, Barrot described the incident as the first large-scale cyberattack conducted for sabotage on French national territory, calling it a major threat to the country’s interests and the security of its population.

“Following its investigation, France is able to attribute these destructive actions to Iran, carried out by the SHAHID KAVEH cyber offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” France’s Foreign Ministry wrote in a Monday statement attributing cyberattacks targeting France to Iran. “This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure.”

It added that these destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law. “They also contravene the principles of the United Nations’ normative framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace, to which the Islamic Republic of Iran has subscribed.”

The agency highlighted that the Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024. In March 2026, the European Union adopted sanctions against the Iranian entity Emmenet Pasargad, which had contributed to conducting these cyberattacks.”

During the night of October 11-12, a cyberattack campaign targeted supermarket refrigeration controllers deployed in over 700 major retail locations across France. These cyberattacks caused considerable material damage, fires, and food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The agency recognized that “this is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory.”

The incident highlights the potential consequences of cyberattacks against connected systems outside traditional IT networks, particularly refrigeration infrastructure used to preserve food supplies and maintain supermarket operations. Reported damage ranged from spoiled inventory and equipment failures, underscoring how attacks on OT (operational technology) infrastructure can translate into direct economic losses and disruption to services relied on by the public.

“In accordance with the 2026 national cybersecurity strategy, France is determined to use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace,” the agency added. “Consequently, France will summon the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to France to express its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks.”

Furthermore, France will propose to its European partners the adoption of new sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved in this cyberattack against it, as well as in other malicious cyber activities.
Finally, France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.
In response, Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as ‘baseless and hostile.’

topic_focus.summary_zh: 黄仁勋因个人丑闻辞职后，在特朗普政府以“国家经济安全与AI开源生态保护”为由的强力干预下火速复职。此举引发了华尔街的疯狂追捧，但也暴露了美系核心科技企业与白宫政治势力深度捆绑、凌驾于公司治理规则之上的巨大争议。
topic_focus.summary_en: Following his resignation due to scandal, Jensen Huang was swiftly reinstated as Nvidia CEO amid direct intervention from the Trump administration, citing national economic security and open-weight AI protection. The move sparked massive market rallies but raised intense ethical questions about the dangerous entanglement of Silicon Valley governance and political power.

perspective_pro.point_en: Argue that Huang is indispensable to US AI dominance; in a critical compute race, the stability of the ecosystem outweighs internal corporate ethics.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: DevOps 架构师及资深工程师

news.title_en: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say

news.author: Emmy Martin
news.content_snippet:
A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device at the company captured dozens of internal meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Monday.

The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, sorted into folders by date and renamed according to their contents, prosecutors said. Many of the recordings involved what appeared to be con
news.summary_en: Federal prosecutors disclosed in court filings that former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan used OpenAI’s Codex AI tool to configure recording devices, capturing dozens of confidential meetings, including sensitive discussions with a foreign government. While data exfiltration remains under investigation, the act constitutes a significant breach of trade secrets and attorney-client privilege.
paragraphs: A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device at the company captured dozens of internal meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Monday.

The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, sorted into folders by date and renamed according to their contents, prosecutors said. Many of the recordings involved what appeared to be confidential trade secrets, including meetings with OpenAI customers, they said, and OpenAI identified others as containing material protected by attorney-client privilege.

The filing, which opposes Mr. Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before trial, offers the most detailed account yet of what investigators say he recorded. It also comes days after prosecutors told a federal judge that they were “not aware of any” evidence that Mr. Alfozan had committed espionage, stolen trade secrets or acted as an agent of a foreign government.
Prosecutors did not say in Monday’s filing that he had shared the recordings with anyone. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation,” they wrote.

Mr. Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, has been charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations and has pleaded not guilty. A hearing on his release is scheduled for Tuesday morning.

His lawyer, David Rizk, argued in a filing last week that the case had turned out to be far less serious than prosecutors initially suggested, describing his client as “an overly curious tinkerer.” Mr. Rizk wrote that the vast majority of recordings on Mr. Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”
Mr. Rizk could not be immediately reached for comment on Monday.

According to prosecutors, the recordings span 15 folders dated Sept. 8 to Sept. 28 and include meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room. One file was titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify the foreign government.

Mr. Alfozan used Codex, an OpenAI A.I. tool, through his wife’s account to help configure the recording device, add voice detection so it would “only record speech,” and move recordings through a Dropbox account, prosecutors said. His wife has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Prosecutors also said he photographed each printed page of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company in the early hours of Oct. 5. That was the same day a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team had found the listening device days earlier.

The filing also described Mr. Alfozan’s contact with Saudi officials. On Oct. 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent him a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based A.I. company, and asked: “Time to move back to KSA and join us?”

Mr. Alfozan suggested he might do so “after the IPO,” prosecutors said. The night before his Oct. 9 arrest, he spoke with the Saudi official by WhatsApp for 16 minutes. Prosecutors said he had also exchanged WhatsApp messages with officials at Saudi Arabia’s communications ministry, including the minister in August and September.

news.title: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges
news.title_en: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges

inline_images.caption: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges (Source: Wall Street Journal)
inline_images.caption_en: France, U.S. Suspect Iran Was Behind Cyberattack on European Fridges (Source: Wall Street Journal)

news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.content_snippet:
French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot
news.summary_en: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot officially attributed the cyberattack on over 700 European supermarket refrigeration controllers to Iran's 'SHAHID KAVEH' cyber unit during a G7 meeting. The attack, occurring between October 11-12, caused widespread equipment failures, fires, and tens of millions of euros in food losses, marking a transition from espionage to physical infrastructure sabotage.
paragraphs: French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Tehran of orchestrating the attack, warning that Iran would face retribution. Speaking Monday at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Paris, Barrot described the incident as the first large-scale cyberattack conducted for sabotage on French national territory, calling it a major threat to the country’s interests and the security of its population.

“Following its investigation, France is able to attribute these destructive actions to Iran, carried out by the SHAHID KAVEH cyber offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” France’s Foreign Ministry wrote in a Monday statement attributing cyberattacks targeting France to Iran. “This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure.”

It added that these destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law. “They also contravene the principles of the United Nations’ normative framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace, to which the Islamic Republic of Iran has subscribed.”

The agency highlighted that the Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024. In March 2026, the European Union adopted sanctions against the Iranian entity Emmenet Pasargad, which had contributed to conducting these cyberattacks.”

During the night of October 11-12, a cyberattack campaign targeted supermarket refrigeration controllers deployed in over 700 major retail locations across France. These cyberattacks caused considerable material damage, fires, and food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The agency recognized that “this is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory.”

The incident highlights the potential consequences of cyberattacks against connected systems outside traditional IT networks, particularly refrigeration infrastructure used to preserve food supplies and maintain supermarket operations. Reported damage ranged from spoiled inventory and equipment failures, underscoring how attacks on OT (operational technology) infrastructure can translate into direct economic losses and disruption to services relied on by the public.

“In accordance with the 2026 national cybersecurity strategy, France is determined to use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace,” the agency added. “Consequently, France will summon the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to France to express its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks.”

Furthermore, France will propose to its European partners the adoption of new sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved in this cyberattack against it, as well as in other malicious cyber activities.
Finally, France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.
In response, Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as ‘baseless and hostile.’

paragraphs: Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue climbed 50% year-over-year to $14.5 billion, topping Wall Street estimates of $14.3 billion.HPE projected Q1 revenue outlook between $14 billion to $14.6 billion, marginally lower than the highest Wall Street estimates of $14.7 billion.The cloud infrastructure firm lifted its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to as high as $63.1 billion.Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (HPE) reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue and profit that surpassed Wall Street expectations on Monday, however, its share price slipped after-hours as its Q1 FY27 outlook fell short of the rosiest of Wall Street expectations.For the quarter ended October 31, the Houston-based technology company posted revenue of $14.5 billion, up 50% from the same period a year earlier and ahead of the $14.3 billion average forecast from analysts polled by Fiscal.ai.

The cloud infrastructure firm reported earnings of $1.43 per share, beating the consensus projection of $1.28 a share. “We are now a fundamentally different company, with greater earnings power, a stronger competitive position, and a portfolio built to capitalize on the next phase of AI,” said Antonio Neri, president and CEO of HPE.

AI Servers And Juniper Integration Drive GrowthHPE’s rapid expansion was anchored by its Cloud & AI division, where quarterly revenue jumped 68.6% year-over-year to $11.3 billion and operating margins nearly doubled to 18.4% from 9.3%. Within that unit, server revenue soared 94.7% to $8.8 billion on the back of demand for systems powered by Nvidia Corp.(NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.(AMD) processors, while storage revenue rose 33.8% to $1.5 billion.

The company’s networking segment, bolstered by its integration of Juniper Networks, generated $3.1 billion in revenue, representing a 12.3% increase over the prior year with an operating profit margin of 22.1%. HPE Fiscal 2027 Earnings GuidanceHPE now projects fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 27% to 35% with revenues reaching as high as $63.1 billion, beating analyst expectations of $55.05 billion.

Full-year adjusted earnings are projected to reach up to $5.35 per share.For the current fiscal first quarter ending in January, HPE forecast revenue between $14 billion and $14.6 billion. While the bottom-line guidance comfortably exceeded Wall Street’s average estimate of $1.08 per share, the top-line range fell just shy of the most bullish analyst projections of $14.7 billion, tempering investor enthusiasm.HPE Stock: Retail View Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘extremely bullish’ with ‘extremely high’ message volumes.

paragraphs: Investing.com -- The European Union and Canada are preparing to outline a broad strategic alliance aimed at deepening economic, defense, and trade ties, according to a report from Bloomberg. The effort reflects an intentional push by middle powers to counter the growing dominance of great-power politics led by the U.S. and China.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is slated to announce the initiative during her annual state of the union address in Strasbourg on Sept. 16. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will attend the speech and is expected to address European lawmakers the following day, underscoring Ottawa's commitment to forging closer integration short of formal EU membership.

The upcoming framework aims to expand cooperation across critical supply chains, raw materials, space exploration, and scientific research. Negotiations are also focused on strengthening joint defense capabilities, building on Ottawa's move last year to become the first non-EU country to participate in the bloc's €150 billion ($174 billion) defense procurement fund.

This diplomatic push follows earlier warnings from Prime Minister Carney, who declared at the World Economic Forum that the traditional rules-based international order has effectively fractured. Against that backdrop, both jurisdictions are seeking structural counterweights to unilateral economic pressure tactics and rising global trade friction.

The alliance builds on an existing bilateral trade agreement and security partnership, with officials exploring how close Canada can legally align with the EU's single market. While discussions remain ongoing regarding necessary regulatory or legal mechanisms, both sides are scheduled to formalize next steps during a joint summit in Canada this October.

paragraphs: After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”
“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.

It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.

Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.

Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday.

News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.

Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”

But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.

The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report, as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.

The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.

The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.

news.title: Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
news.title_en: Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
news.author: Elizabeth Lopatto
news.summary_en:
I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.

paragraphs: I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.

Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now.
"The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy"

I have argued here, in the past, that the Epstein case laid bare the real politics of the revanchist American right wing: total elite impunity. Well, here it is again! If you are close enough with Trump, it doesn’t matter if you may have jeopardized national security by fucking an alleged Chinese spy. You won’t even be investigated for it before the American president calls in to your board of directors’ meeting to demand you be reinstated. I mean, it is the era of gangster tech regulation — what were any of us expecting? The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy, Vance.

Just so we can be absolutely clear about what transpired at Nvidia, let’s quickly go through the facts as we know them. A Chinese citizen named Alice Huang acquired the company she renamed Megaspeed, the Singaporean data firm at the center of this inquiry, in 2023. At some point, Huang met Huang, and the two were seen together at a dinner that December. From 2024 to 2025, Megaspeed received more than 200 Nvidia shipments.

In September 2025, the US government began investigating Megaspeed for possible violations of chip export controls; that October, the State Department told Trump of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, who was described as a Chinese intelligence asset. Also in October, The New York Times first reported on Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia. In December, Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — allowed Nvidia to sell more powerful chips to China. In March 2026, Marco Rubio warned the government about Alice, and Trump nonetheless invited Huang to a visit in China. In October, The New York Times reported on the affair. Shortly after Huang sent a note to Nvidia admitting to it, several other reports of infidelity — this time with Nvidia employees — surfaced. On November 12th, Huang resigned. On November 17th, during the Nvidia earnings call, the board’s chair said that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On November 23rd, Huang was back.
"This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive"

What changed between last week and this week? A week was not enough time to truly review all the information on Huang and his paramour, Alice “No Relation” Huang, the international woman of mystery. The explanation seems to be that Nvidia’s board succumbed to a pressure campaign from Huang’s fellow billionaires, and a direct intervention from the president and vice president of the United States of America.

Sure, all these CEOs ostensibly wanted Huang back at Nvidia to keep the AI trade going. Still, watching the likes of Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, investing loudmouth Bill Ackman, and Elon Musk — who actually did appear in the Epstein files, and who seemed to be pretty friendly with Epstein! — pitch a fit last week was instructive. These men worried that they might be punished for wrongdoing, that they did not get big enough to be above the law. They have now been reassured, and I suppose that is what really matters. After all, Trump said on CNBC that he gave Nvidia’s board assurances that Jensen is “absolutely fine.”

This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive, and not just because Huang is CEO of Nvidia again. Almost in passing, Trump noted that he had “protected” Musk in his first term from “a certain incident [that] took place, a very tough incident.” In his own inimitable style, Trump told Jim Cramer, “You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally.
"Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally"

One thing that has perhaps emboldened this crew is the stance from professional politics-knowers — and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries — that holding members of the Trump administration accountable might be a hindrance to governing. That accountability was part of the reason for the blue wave in November seems to have bypassed these pundits (and the presumptive House majority leader). But then, why should we believe that Democrats will thoroughly investigate this? Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is claiming to want an investigation, but I am skeptical of how deep that investigation will go as long as Schumer leads it, and only partially because he’s been allied with Silicon Valley for more than a decade. He also has a daughter who works at OpenAI, a company that Nvidia invests in and that is dependent on Nvidia chips. How hard is he really willing to go?

Nvidia led a thunderous rally on Wall Street following the surprise return of Jensen Huang, the charismatic and flawed booster for the entire artificial intelligence industry, as the chip company’s CEO. US stocks recovered just over half their brutal loss from last week, which was one of their worst since the 2008 financial crisis.

The S&P 500 surged 4.7 per cent in a demonstration of how much the US stock market depends on just one industry. Rallies for beaten-down AI stocks sent the Nasdaq composite up a market-leading 6.5 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped nearly 1450 points, or 3 per cent.

The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a rise of 128 points or 1.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US66.28¢.

Even before Wall Street opened for the day, trading in the futures market suggested US stocks were set to halt the seven-day losing streak that dragged the S&P 500 more than 10 per cent below its all-time high set last month. Then came the bombshell about Huang’s return to Nvidia, even though its board is still investigating whether he was the target of a foreign spy and created any national-security concerns. That kicked the rally into overdrive.

Nvidia’s stock surged 31.5 per cent and finished just shy of its best day since 2000, close to when the dot-com bubble peaked. That followed its plunge of nearly 23 per cent last week, though it’s still below where it was before Huang’s scandal initially broke.
Stocks closely tied to Nvidia rocketed higher. CoreWeave, a company that buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them over the cloud, shot up 22.3 per cent.

Other stocks in far-flung industries that have benefited from the AI boom likewise recovered some of their losses. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, rose 8.2 per cent following last week’s drop of nearly 13 per cent. Caterpillar, whose sales of equipment have benefited because of the construction boom around AI, climbed 7.2 per cent after sinking 15 per cent last week.

How AI-related stocks do matters incredibly for workers’ 401(k) accounts because Nvidia and other chip stocks have grown into some of Wall Street’s largest and most influential. Coming into the day, a 1 per cent swing for Nvidia’s stock carried more of an effect on the S&P 500 than a 1 per cent move for all but two of the 500 companies in the index.

Monday’s rebound for the S&P 500 was its best day since April of 2025, which is when President Donald Trump paused most of his tariffs announced on “Liberation Day” that had sent stock markets reeling. Trump may have had direct influence on this most recent surge as well.

paragraphs: An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts

OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.
### How Shirudo works

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:
Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

paragraphs: The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”

To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.

“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.

Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice).
With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever.

To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.

Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency.

“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event.

In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found.

To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation.

OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. news.summary_en: OpenAI has officially rolled out the GPT-6.2 model to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Business users. This iteration delivers significant enhancements in multimodal understanding and instruction following, outperforming its predecessor in expert-level reasoning tasks while demonstrating marked improvements in safety policy compliance, particularly regarding youth protection.
paragraphs: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).

On an internal benchmark for expert-level tasks, GPT-6.2 beats GPT-6 across all four reasoning levels, according to OpenAI. It scores roughly 65 to just over 71 percent, compared with about 52 to 66 percent for GPT-6. OpenAI also uses an internal version of BrowseComp to test how well models find answers to tough questions on the web. GPT-6.2 leads at every level, finishing about 10 percentage points ahead at the highest one.

According to the system card, GPT-6.2 follows safety policies in 91 to 94 percent of difficult conversations, up from 77 to 80 percent for GPT-6. The model makes its biggest gains in youth safety, specifically around emotional dependency, eating disorders, and dangerous activities.
These numbers only apply to ChatGPT's chat mode. The Work and Codex models stay the same. Enterprise admins can decide whether their users get access to GPT-6.2.

news.author: Ashley Gold
news.summary_en:
The Trump administration plans to add the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The Singapore-based company will be added to the Commerce Department’s entity list on Monday, the sources said.

paragraphs: The Trump administration plans to add the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Singapore-based company will be added to the Commerce Department’s entity list on Monday, the sources said.

The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the department’s entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.

Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list “for months” but that “Commerce holds the pen.” Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.

"He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said.
Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said.

paragraphs: Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.

Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.

PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

news.title: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
news.title_en: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
news.author: Emma Roth
news.summary_en:
The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago co-founded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. paragraphs: The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago co-founded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”

Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman, Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.

So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said during an earnings call last week.

But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left.

The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders began posting in support of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney questioned the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s departure to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage, “it’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.”
“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said.

Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit. Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty, telling reporters, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had relied on US intelligence sources.

Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s shares crashed following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO, something industry analysts speculated would prove exceptionally difficult. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry.

Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place, before saying that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back.

This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A report from The New York Times says that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.” Semafor reports that Trump even called into Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.”

Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it reinstated Huang as its CEO, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He added in a post on Truth Social that the US Attorney General confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

news.summary_en: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, just 11 days after his resignation amid scandal and foreign intelligence investigation. U.S. leadership intervened to secure his return, viewing him as the indispensable protector of the American open-weight AI ecosystem and a critical instrument for maintaining technical leverage against China.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

Open-weight AI models are systems whose core components are publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Their growth has become a major business opportunity for Nvidia because they broaden demand for the company's chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of large AI developers.

China leads in the development of open-weight AI systems, which are gaining ground with US companies because they can be cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic . They can also perform nearly as well.

Nvidia has been one of the most prominent backers of the US open-weight ecosystem. Nvidia in August agreed to buy the company Hugging Face, a platform that developers use to host open-weight AI models, among other AI-related resources. Nvidia is also an investor in Reflection AI, an American company that launched its first open-weight model in October.

Huang and Nvidia's lobbyists have also pressed US lawmakers to support the development of open-weight AI technology, with Huang writing in a letter earlier this year that they should avoid "premature restrictions" on such tools.
Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports that he engaged in several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on November 18 that the Trump administration was considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, including open-weight models, as part of an effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology.

Republican lawmakers have increasingly echoed the argument that open-weight AI is critical to competing with China. Two leading House Republican lawmakers on Friday called on the Trump administration to help American companies developing open-weight AI models, adding that it would position the US to better counter China.

news.title: Adyen Co CEO Pieter Van Der Does To Retire From Payments Firm
news.title_en: Adyen Co CEO Pieter Van Der Does To Retire From Payments Firm
news.author: Bloomberg
news.summary_en:
Adyen has turned its payment processing business into one of Europe's biggest entrepreneurial success stories. Now it's quietly deploying artificial intelligence to keep its remarkable growth streak going.

paragraphs: Adyen has turned its payment processing business into one of Europe's biggest entrepreneurial success stories. Now it's quietly deploying artificial intelligence to keep its remarkable growth streak going.

The Amsterdam-based company's philosophy of building tools from within rather than through acquisitions has been crucial to its rise, from its founding in 2006 to its 2018 IPO. Its approach to AI reflects that same philosophy. The company hasn't been talking much about its work in this area but has been cautiously deploying its algorithms internally.

Adyen CEO Pieter van der Does told VentureBeat that the company has studiously avoided hype-driven trends and so initially took a conservative approach to AI. But after developing in-house fraud-detection algorithms, van der Does was quickly convinced of AI's potential.
"When we did our first trials with it, I was surprised how effective it was," he said.
He spoke to VentureBeat as part of a podcasting partnership with Samsung Next at the Slush technology conference in Helsinki, Finland. The full conversation can be heard here.

As hype around AI began to build, van der Does' natural reaction was to be dubious. Rather than panicking and rushing to acquire a startup for its technology, the company began building its own algorithms internally. The results almost immediately exceeded expectations. "The benefits of AI are real," van der Does said.

Adyen is using AI for fraud detection. That has allowed the company to better leverage the large number of data points its system absorbs to make faster and more accurate decisions about people's creditworthiness. Its risk management service -- called RevenueProtect -- includes a ShoperDNA feature, which allows for real-time identification of shoppers.

With AI, Adyen has been able to expand the data points and methodology, which in turn enables much more granular examination of a person or pattern when a purchase is being made. Its Risk Engine automates transaction reviews, which reduces review times by 30%, according to the company.
Typically, such fraud detection is measured by how it limits losses. But van der Does said it's just as important to measure additional transactions that are approved.

He used the example of an Israeli software developer who works in New York and sends a purchase to Europe with a credit card issued in Israel. There's a good chance that such a transaction might be flagged or blocked. But with AI able to process more detail, it might realize that the developer is just sending flowers and the transaction is probably fine.

This way of incorporating AI fits with Adyen's solid, problem-solving approach. The company isn't trying to spin itself as some machine learning-driven wonder. Instead, it treats AI as a practical advance.

"Risk in payments is a way to raise authorization dollars," he said. "If you allow the transaction, your merchant has more revenue than [they] would have had with the old system. That is good for everyone."

OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

news.summary_en: OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki revealed the log-perplexity scores for models from GPT-3.5 to GPT-6 and beyond, illustrating how capabilities emerge as metrics improve. This initiative aims to establish a common industry performance standard to encourage rivals to coordinate development pacing at critical safety thresholds.
paragraphs: OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

Pachocki wants to make perplexity a common measure of progress for the AI industry and published internal scores for the GPT series in a bl o g post. The metric has long been standard in AI research and Transformer development because it reliably measures how well a pretrained base model predicts the next token in a text.
Lower scores mean more accurate predictions. A perplexity of 2 roughly means the model is as uncertain about the next token as if it were choosing between two equally likely options.

Before it stopped publishing openly, OpenAI often released perplexity scores to show how its models were improving. Releasing them again is a trade-off, Pachocki writes. While rivals get a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands, he says, the need for shared safety standards outweighs that downside. He hopes for a common scientific foundation that lets labs coordinate their pace of development at critical points.
### Capabilities emerge at distinct perplexity thresholds

Pachocki says many capabilities of modern models map surprisingly closely to specific perplexity scores, even though it wasn't clear beforehand that they would appear at those thresholds. He reports the figures on a logarithmic scale called log-perplexity, where lower scores are still better. In his account, GPT-3.5 first enabled fluent conversation at around 0.99, laying the groundwork for the original ChatGPT. At about 0.91, GPT-4 unlocked productive chain-of-thought reasoning, or working through problems step by step. Below 0.8, he writes, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and math.

The published chart plots OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity by release or evaluation date through November 2026. It covers GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Astra, plus an internal model at around 0.73.
### OpenAI's models deliver math breakthroughs in a Slack thread

OpenAI has been feeding its models open math problems for more than a year. Starting with a model at about 0.76 log-perplexity, the models began producing breakthrough results, Pachocki writes. For researchers with a math background, he says, it was "deeply surreal"to watch solutions to longstanding questions pop up one after another in a single Slack thread.

Those results include a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the Millennium Prize problems, though it hasn't been fully verified yet. The same goes for the proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis found by Claude and an Anthropic researcher. Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training.

A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post.

news.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
news.title_en: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
news.author: Jess Weatherbed
news.summary_en: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” desc
paragraphs: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”

The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.

xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.
Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.

news.title: Nvidia’s About-Face on Huang Made Without Consulting Leadership
news.title_en: Nvidia’s About-Face on Huang Made Without Consulting Leadership
news.author: Zeus Kerravala
news.summary_en:
Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executi
paragraphs: Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.
### 1. The machine will run without the founder

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

paragraphs: Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.

The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value, until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the last month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia's board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?

The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.

On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.

Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amidst the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it actually. The stock is up.”
According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.
“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

news.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
news.title_en: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
news.author: James Donnell
news.summary_en:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
